source.title: The jamming transition as a paradigm to understand the loss landscape of deep neural networks
source.authors: M. Geiger; Stefano Spigler; Stéphane d'Ascoli; Levent Sagun; Marco Baity-Jesi; G. Biroli; M. Wyart

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether fully connected networks can fit random data and whether depth affects that ability, using a capacity sweep and a jamming-transition analysis.
record.gate_note: The study trains on synthetic inputs with random binary labels and reports a fit transition. It does not report test error on random labels or compare true and randomized labels on the same images. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures whether fully connected networks trained by gradient methods fit completely random binary labels on synthetic inputs, using a capacity sweep and a jamming-transition analysis.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors find a sharp fitting transition controlled mainly by parameter count, with little depth dependence in the tested fully connected networks. They interpret its landscape geometry as hypostatic jamming and argue, under assumptions about effective parameters and curvature, that sufficiently overparametrized networks cannot become trapped in poor minima.
record.recipe_differences: Uses synthetic random inputs as well as random labels, binary classification, and a width sweep to study a fit transition; compares cross-entropy/SGD and hinge/ADAM settings rather than reproducing random relabeling of images.
record.method_sensitivity: The transition location has a mild dependence on the dynamics, including optimizer, batch size, and learning-rate schedule; the study reports little dependence on depth or input dimension in the tested cross-entropy experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: The parameter threshold for fitting is largely independent of depth for random data and PCA-reduced MNIST; MNIST requires fewer parameters than random data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For these fully connected networks and training protocols, data structure affects the fitting capacity threshold more than depth does.

record.problems: Synthetic random inputs and labels do not directly establish fitting of randomly relabeled images. The study varies width to locate the transition, and the reported transition plots do not provide tabulated numerical values in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Chance-level test error and fitting randomly relabeled data without changing the architecture or training hyperparameters used for true labels are not established.
No comparison of training time for true versus random labels, or convergence time across corrupted-label fractions.
No experiments on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs; the synthetic inputs lie on a hypersphere.
No corruption-fraction sweep or corresponding training and test error curves.
No controlled tests of weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation, or of true-label generalization after removing these.
No comparison of the temporal learning order of shared real-data patterns and noisy labels.

missing.what: Separate the cross-entropy training-time conditions: at large P and short times errors persist and no fitting transition is found; longer training approaches N* proportional to P.

Add the quantitative random-data hinge experiment with N approximately 8,000, depths 2, 3 and 5, and up to 10^7 steps: unsatisfied constraints vanish for P/N below 2.8, remain above 0.7N for P/N above 2.9, and have not converged between these values. Keep margin violations distinct from classification errors.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source of these versions. Synthetic inputs do not invalidate the direct V1 fitting test. Missing chance-test-error and unchanged-recipe comparisons are untested components, not evidence against V1. Positive hinge loss alone does not establish classification error, because correctly classified examples can still violate the margin.

versions.untested_parts: Tests fitting synthetic random inputs with random labels as network size varies. Does not test random relabeling of training images, test error at chance, or a fixed architecture and hyperparameter comparison.
Does not compare training time for true versus random labels or measure convergence time as a function of corrupted-label fraction.
Does not test shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Does not sweep the fraction of corrupted labels or report test error across corruption levels.
Does not test weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation as controls on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
Does not compare learning of real-label patterns and random labels over training.

rows.measure: Training fit transition as parameter count N is reduced; N* versus number of data P.
rows.value: The transition appears to scale as N* ~ P; above it the loss becomes null, below it the loss remains non-zero. The transition does not appear to depend on L and d.
rows.note: The study reports a transition in synthetic random-data experiments; text describes the empirical scaling and depth/dimension independence, while plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Observed applies to sufficiently large networks with enough training time. Replace the claim that cross-entropy loss becomes null with zero training classification error: Section III explicitly states that cross-entropy remains positive at finite weights. Record batch normalization and the learning-rate schedule. Separate unsuccessful small-width or short-training conditions from successful fitting.

source_check.correct: At sufficiently long training times, N* scales approximately linearly with P. Above the fitting threshold, training classification error is zero; cross-entropy loss remains positive for finite outputs. Split successful configurations (observed) from insufficient-width or insufficient-time configurations with persistent classification errors.
source_check.locator_found: Section III, lines 618–648 and 659–670; Fig. 5(a,b), lines 562–568.
source_check.problem: The value confuses zero classification error with zero cross-entropy loss; the unconditional observed state combines successful and unsuccessful configurations.

rows.measure: Training fit transition as parameter count N is reduced; N* versus number of data P.
rows.value: The transition location is reported as very similar to that for cross-entropy; above the transition all data are fitted.
rows.note: The text characterizes the hinge-loss results as very similar to cross-entropy; plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Observed applies above the fitting threshold. The loss is quadratic hinge loss; training uses orthogonal initialization, no batch normalization, and a learning rate initially 10^-4 divided by ten every 250,000 steps. Separate unsuccessful small-width conditions from successful fitting.

source_check.correct: The quadratic-hinge transition location is very similar to the cross-entropy result. Zero loss and perfect classification occur above the threshold; reducing width eventually prevents perfect classification within the training budget. Split successful configurations (observed) from unsuccessful configurations.

source_check.problem: The unconditional observed state does not distinguish the successful and unsuccessful portions of the width sweep.

tranche.reason: Directly tests random-label fitting through synthetic binary classification, width sweeps, and a jamming analysis using different losses and optimization protocols.
